candidates.structure: A stat-and-chart explainer: title, big number, bar chart, closing. Clear, but the same skeleton as most data videos.
candidates.why: Safe, and it hides the argument inside the numbers.

candidates.structure: A bill that keeps growing: one measured quantity shown at three scales (world, one country, the forecast), each drawn as its own picture, ending on the uncertainty.
candidates.why: The argument is the growth and the doubt, so the pictures should grow and then blur.

candidates.structure: A list of objections, one scene each: electricity, water, emissions, local grids.
candidates.why: Covers more, but water and local-grid figures were not verified, so those scenes would rest on claims I cannot source.

treatment.logline: Data-centre power demand is set to double, is concentrated in two countries, and even the forecasts disagree by more than two to one.
treatment.opening: A title that asks who is counting the power behind every answer, then one big measured number in the first seconds.
treatment.signature: The forecast range for 2035: a track with three markers (700, 1,200 and 1,700 TWh) and a bar spanning them, drawn freeform so the width of the doubt is what you see.
treatment.ending: Returns to the opening question: ask where the power comes from.

scenes.say: Every chatbot answer runs on electricity. Who is counting?

scenes.label: used by data centres in 2024: about 1.5% of the world's electricity
scenes.say: In 2024, data centres used about four hundred and fifteen terawatt-hours.
By 2030 the IEA expects that to roughly double.

scenes.label: of the world's electricity in 2030: small, but growing fast
scenes.say: Still just under three percent of the world's electricity, but growing fast.

scenes.caption: US data centres, TWh a year. 2028 is a projected range (Berkeley Lab / DOE, 2024).
scenes.say: In the US, 58 terawatt-hours in 2014 became 176 in 2023, and up to 580 by 2028.

elements.text: Share of global growth in data-centre demand to 2030

scenes.say: Nearly eighty percent of that growth is in just two countries: China and the United States.
For 2035, the IEA's own scenarios run from 700 to 1,700 terawatt-hours.

scenes.label: the gap between the IEA's low and high 2035 cases
scenes.say: Planning a grid around a range that wide is closer to guessing.

scenes.title: Ask where the power comes from
points: Nearly 80% of growth: China and the US
scenes.say: Before the next data centre is approved, ask where the power comes from.
